summary: This informational memo evaluates how well SNMP, RSIP, Megaco, Diameter and COPS could serve as the protocol for middlebox communications, which lets applications talk to devices like firewalls. It compares each candidate against the requirements.

plainLanguage.summary: The MIDCOM working group needed one protocol for letting an application ask a firewall or a NAT to let a call through. Five candidate protocols were put forward, and each was marked against every requirement in turn.

questions: which protocol was best for midcom
subtitle: A scorecard of five existing protocols against the requirements for talking to firewalls and NATs.

tldr.problem: The MIDCOM working group needed a protocol that lets an application-aware agent control middleboxes such as firewalls and NATs, and had to choose an existing one rather than invent a new one.
tldr.mechanism: Volunteers wrote evaluations of SNMP, RSIP, Megaco, Diameter and COPS. Each protocol was scored requirement by requirement as totally compliant, partially compliant through extensions, partially compliant, or failing.
tldr.outcome: None of the five failed any requirement. SNMP scored best with 22 fully met, RSIP was not accepted by the working group because of tunneling, and the RFC says the table is input to a decision, not a verdict.

today: RFC 4097 is an Informational RFC from June 2005. It provides a record of how the MIDCOM protocol candidates compared and does not specify an Internet standard of any kind, and it has been updated by RFC 8996. Its security considerations are covered by the comparison against the MIDCOM security requirements in sections 2.1.8 and 2.3.

sections.title: What Was Evaluated and Why
sections.content:
MIDCOM stands for Middlebox Communications. The evaluation looks at five protocols as candidates for the MIDCOM protocol: SNMP, RSIP, Megaco, Diameter and COPS. Each protocol was examined for how well it fits the MIDCOM framework in RFC 3303 and the MIDCOM requirements in RFC 3304.

The process was straightforward: individuals volunteered to write a document evaluating one specific protocol, and those documents were submitted for discussion on the working group list, with feedback incorporated into updated versions that formed the basis of this document. The RFC is candid about the limits of that method. Some protocols that might be considered as reasonably applicable are not evaluated, because there were no volunteers to champion the work.

The document has four parts. Section 1 describes each proposed protocol with background information and its similarities and differences with respect to the MIDCOM framework. Section 2 evaluates the protocols item by item against the requirements. Section 3 summarises the evaluation with a numerical breakdown per protocol, and says plainly that the summary is not meant to provide a conclusive statement of the suitability of the protocols but rather information to be considered as input into the overall protocol decision process. The appendices carry the background detail on the protocols and on the enhancements and applications proposed to make them comply.
sections.plainLanguage: An application sometimes needs to politely ask a firewall for help. This memo compares five existing ways of talking to such devices and scores each of them against the rules the group had written down.

sections.title: The Four Compliance Marks
sections.content:
Each protocol was reviewed against every MIDCOM requirement, grouped into protocol machinery, protocol semantics and general security requirements, and each result given one of four marks. T is total compliance, meaning the requirement is met fully. P+ is partial compliance plus: the requirement is fundamentally met through the use of extensions such as packages or additional parameters. P is partial compliance, where some aspect of the requirement is met but the necessary changes require more than an extension, or are inconsistent with the design intent of the protocol. F is failed compliance, meaning the requirement is not met.

Security considerations for the MIDCOM protocol are covered by this comparison against the specific security requirements in the MIDCOM requirements document, and are specifically addressed by the evaluation of the protocol machinery requirements in section 2.1.8 and of the general security requirements in section 2.3.
sections.plainLanguage: Every protocol was marked against every requirement, and each mark says how well that requirement was met: fully, fully with an extension, only in part, or not at all.

sections.title: SNMP as the MIDCOM Protocol
sections.content:
The SNMP evaluation is specific to SNMPv3, which provides the security that MIDCOM usage requires; SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c would be inappropriate because they have been declared Historic and their messages have only trivial security. The primary advantages of SNMPv3 are that it is a mature, well understood protocol, already deployed in various scenarios, with mature toolsets available for managers and agents. SNMPv3 keeps the separation of data modelling, in MIB modules, from the protocol that transfers the data, so the messaging protocol carries the data in a standardised format without needing to understand its semantics, and the endpoints understand the semantics. It uses the SMIv2 standard and shares operations and transport with SNMPv2c, and the major difference from earlier versions is the addition of strong message security and controlled access to data.

Because monitoring can be done with a least-common-denominator subset of information across vendors, many MIB modules were developed for monitoring, and SNMP has been used primarily for monitoring rather than for configuring network nodes. For configuring NATs, a NAT MIB module already exists and meets all of the MIDCOM requirements concerning NAT control with the exception of grouping of policy rules, requirement 2.2.3, which needs an additional grouping table. For firewalls, the existing SNMP work only considered monitoring and not configuration, so further work is needed towards MIBs for configuring firewalls.

There are architectural differences to reconcile. The SNMP Manager corresponds to the MIDCOM agent and the SNMP Agent to the MIDCOM Policy Decision Point, and the evaluation assumes that the MIDCOM Policy Decision Point, which is the SNMP Agent, is physically part of the middlebox. To implement MIDCOM on SNMP, a MIDCOM MIB module is required: all requests from the MIDCOM agent to the middlebox are performed using write access to the managed objects in that module, and replies are signalled by the middlebox modifying those managed objects, which the MIDCOM agent can pick up by reading or polling. The use of a proxy agent or mid-level manager is not considered, because proxy adds configuration and deployment complexity and is not needed to meet the requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP is a long-used way to read and set dials on devices, so it would need a new set of dials for firewalls. The request becomes a write to one of those dials, and the answer comes back as a change to another.

sections.title: RSIP and Its Limits
sections.content:
The RSIP framework and protocol are defined in RFC 3102 and RFC 3103. Several framework elements are common to MIDCOM and RSIP, listed under their MIDCOM names with the RSIP name in brackets: hosts, applications, middleboxes, which are RSIP gateways, the private domain, which is the private realm, the external domain, which is the public realm, the middlebox communication protocol, agent registration, which is host registration, the session, and the filter, which is a pair of local or remote address and port numbers.

Three MIDCOM elements are not supported by RSIP. Policy actions and rules are among them, because RSIP always implicitly assumes a permit action and a more general, explicit action parameter would have to be defined. RSIP also makes no distinction between applications and agents, so address assignment operations can be performed equally by either. And RSIP assumes that middleboxes grant or deny requests with reference to a policy known to them, without addressing joint determination with a policy decision point.

Several elements are unique to RSIP and would have to be added to the MIDCOM framework if RSIP were adopted: the RSIP client, which is the part of an application or agent that talks to the gateway; the RSIP server, which is the part of the gateway that talks to applications; the Realm Specific Address IP and Realm Specific Address and Port IP, which distinguish filters that include all ports on an address from those that do not; and the demultiplexing fields a gateway uses to route an incoming packet. The evaluation also worked through the tunneling that RSIP needs between the host and the middlebox, and the conclusion section records that this tunneling results in RSIP not being acceptable by the working group as the MIDCOM protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: RSIP is a way of lending your computer an outside address, and it turned out to need too many changes before it could do the job.

sections.title: Megaco, Diameter and COPS
sections.content:
Megaco is a master-slave, transaction-oriented protocol in which Media Gateway Controllers control the operation of Media Gateways. It was originally designed to control IP telephony gateways, and it is used between an application-unaware device, the Media Gateway, and an application-aware entity, the Media Gateway Controller. Its model has several key concepts: terminations, which are logical entities on the gateway acting as sources or sinks of packet streams; contexts, which associate terminations for sharing media; virtual media gateways, which let one physical gateway be partitioned so several controllers can work with disjoint sets of contexts; transactions and messages, where each command applies to one termination in a context and generates a unique response; descriptors and properties; events and signals; and packages, which group properties and events and are the means of extending the protocol to serve various types of middlebox. The Media Gateway Controller resembles the MIDCOM agent and the Media Gateway resembles the middlebox, but there is a major difference: MIDCOM requires the MIDCOM agent to establish the session, whereas in Megaco the gateway establishes communication with the controller.

Diameter is designed to support authentication, authorization and accounting for network access. Endpoints are either clients, which perform network access control, or servers, which handle the requests for a realm, and intermediate nodes relay, proxy, redirect and translate. Messages consist of a header and an aggregation of strongly typed Attribute-Value Pairs, and one of the types in the base protocol is the IPFilterRule, which may be enough to express the policy rules that MIDCOM deals with. The protocol is connection-oriented at both the transport and application levels and tied closely to sessions. The evaluation found a good overall fit, with the MIDCOM agent not performing the functions of a Diameter client and the middlebox not supporting the functions of a Diameter server, but noted that the connection orientation may be too heavy for the number of relationships the middlebox must support, and that much of the Diameter base is surplus to the MIDCOM requirements.

COPS is a simple query and response protocol for exchanging policy information between a policy server, the Policy Decision Point, and its clients, the Policy Enforcement Points. It uses TCP, it is extensible through self-identifying objects, it was created for the general administration, configuration and enforcement of policies, and it offers message-level security for authentication, replay protection and message integrity, optionally using IPsec or TLS to secure the channel. It is stateful in that request and decision state is kept synchronised between client and server, and in that the server can push configuration to the client and later remove it. Here too the middlebox serves as the client and the MIDCOM agent as the policy server, and here too the model has the client establishing the session, which is the opposite of what MIDCOM requires.
sections.plainLanguage: Megaco and COPS both expect the device at the edge to open the conversation, while MIDCOM expects the application-aware agent to do it. Diameter fits the requirements but carries much more machinery than this application needs.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.content:
Across all the requirements, no protocol failed any. SNMP scored 22 fully met and 5 partially met through extensions, RSIP 17, 7 and 3, Megaco 19, 5 and 3, Diameter 21, 5 and 1, and COPS 20, 5 and 2. The extension mechanism matters as much as the counts. SNMP and COPS-PR extend through MIBs and PIBs with no impact on the protocol, while Diameter extensions and Megaco's packages both require protocol changes that the sending and receiving entities must understand, and the RSIP extension mechanism has the largest impact because it is based on defining new parameters.

The SNMP management framework meets all the specified MIDCOM protocol requirements with the appropriate design of a MIDCOM MIB module. SNMP is a proven technology with stable development tools, already has extensions defined to support NAT configuration and policy-based management, and SNMPv3 is a full standard that has been deployed to manage large-scale real-world networks. Its restriction is that it assumes the MIDCOM Policy Decision Point is part of the middlebox. RSIP fully meets many requirements but needs additions and extensions, would need several framework elements added to the MIDCOM framework, and its tunneling results in RSIP not being acceptable by the working group as the MIDCOM protocol. Megaco fully meets most of the key requirements but would need a new termination and package definition. The Diameter evaluation indicated a good overall fit, with some partially met requirements that could be addressed by a new application extension, but the architecture may be too heavy and much of the base is not needed; it was also the only protocol whose RFCs had not yet been published at the time of the evaluation. COPS meets the majority of the requirements using its own extension techniques, but to fully satisfy one partially met requirement the COPS model would need to allow a Policy Decision Point to establish communication with a Policy Enforcement Point, which would require additions in the form of local policy.
sections.plainLanguage: No candidate failed a single requirement. SNMP met the most of them outright, RSIP was ruled out because of its tunnelling, and the RFC is careful to say that the table is input to a decision rather than the decision itself.

items.title: T
items.text: Total compliance. The requirement is met fully.

items.title: P+
items.text: Partial compliance plus. The requirement is fundamentally met through extensions such as packages or additional parameters.

items.title: P
items.text: Partial compliance. Some aspect is met, but the changes need more than an extension or conflict with the design intent.

items.title: F
items.text: Failed compliance. The requirement is not met.
